chunks: Ibn Mahboub, from Abdullah ibn Ghalib, from his father, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who said:

I heard Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) saying: 'A man came to Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) and said, 'Inform me, if you are knowledgeable, about the people, and about those who resemble the people, and about the Nasnas.' So Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) said, 'O Husayn, answer the man.'
So al-Husayn (peace be upon him) said: 'As for your word,
Then hasten on from the place from which the people hasten on

so it is the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) who caused the people to hasten forth. And as for your word, 'those who resemble the people,' they are our Shias, and they are our friends, and they are from us.
And that is what Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said: 'Then whoever follows me is surely of me.'
And as for your word, 'the Nasnas,' they are the vast majority.
They are nothing but as cattle; nay, they are straying farther off from the path
and he gestured by his hand towards a group of the people.

key_terms.النَّاسُ: The People (specifically Ahl al-Bayt in this context)
key_terms.النَّسْنَاسُ: The Nasnas (a term for the vast majority/general public)

ai.seo_question: What is the meaning of Nasnas in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Kafi presents a hierarchical cosmology of humanity rooted in Shia theology, where Imam Ali (as) categorizes people into three tiers: the Ahl al-Bayt as the true 'people,' their Shias as their 'resemblers,' and the general masses (Nasnas) as the 'vast majority' who are spiritually akin to cattle. By linking these categories to specific Quranic verses, the narration emphasizes the spiritual authority of the Imams and the distinct status of their followers, while critiquing the majority's lack of deep insight. This classification underscores the Shia view of divine guidance being concentrated within the Prophet's household and their loyal adherents.
